generator.params.joints.why: Chollas, prickly pears and the jointed epiphytes grow as chains of joints.

generator.params.pad.why: A prickly pear's or a Christmas cactus's joints are flat.

generator.params.joint_radius.why: A joint's radius, or a pad's half width.

generator.params.teeth.why: A toothed joint's margins are cut into as many saw teeth a side as its flora gives.

appearance.organs.flower.form.flower.cup.why: A cactus's tepals are free, on a spiral that runs from the spreading outer ones to the upright inner ones about this mean rise: flat in a wheel, a bowl in a cup, a bell, a funnel, a narrow tube, a flat limb on a tube, an urn.

appearance.organs.*.shape.tube.why: A cactus's tepals stand on the rim of a floral tube, the hypanthium grown up round the ovary: barely any in a wheel or a cup, as Opuntia's flowers have none above the pericarpel, short in a bell, longer in a funnel, longest in a tube or under a salver's limb; in flower radii. Where the flora gives the flower's length as well as its width (its 'flowers 1.5-5 × 1.5-5 cm', length by width), the tube is what the length leaves beyond the tepals' rise, so a flower 'two times wider than long' (Flora of North America's Ariocarpus fissuratus) sits low in its wool.

appearance.organs.*.shape.petal_width.why: A cactus's inner tepals are broad and overlap at their bases in a wheel or a cup, a little narrower in a bell or a funnel, and narrow in a tube.

appearance.organs.*.shape.pericarpel.why: A cactus's ovary is sunk in its stem tissue, the pericarpel, which wears on the flower and on the bud below the closed tepals what it will wear as a fruit: nothing on a pincushion's, broad scales on a barrel's or the saguaro's, felted areoles on a prickly pear's, spiny areoles on a hedgehog's (Anderson, The Cactus Family pp. 27 to 33, 139, 231, 328 and 486).

appearance.organs.*.shape.spines_fall.why: A spiny cactus fruit whose spine clusters fall as it ripens (FNA vol. 4: Stenocereus 'bearing deciduous spine clusters', Echinocereus 'spine clusters usually deciduous at maturity') is drawn ripe with its felted areoles alone.

appearance.organs.*.shape.pericarpel_col.why: A cactus's pericarpel is a joint of its stem round the sunk ovary, so it is drawn in the colour its flora gives the stem: a beavertail's blue-grey, a cholla's green (Anderson, The Cactus Family pp. 25 to 27).

appearance.organs.*.shape.pericarpel_fel.why: A cactus pericarpel's areoles are the stem's, felted in the wool its flora gives the stem's areoles (Anderson, The Cactus Family pp. 25 to 27).

appearance.organs.*.shape.felt.why: A cactus fruit is its pericarpel grown on, and its areoles are felted as the stem's are.

appearance.organs.*.shape.pericarpel_bri.why: A spiny pericarpel's spines are coloured as the stem's spines; a felted one's tufts are glochids, coloured as its flora gives the glochids (a beavertail's reddish brown).

appearance.organs.*.shape.bristles.why: A spiny cactus fruit's spines are coloured as the stem's spines; a felted one's tufts are glochids, coloured as its flora gives the glochids.

appearance.organs.*.shape.kind.why: A cactus's fruit is its pericarpel grown on, crowned by the dried perianth: naked in a pincushion's, under broad scales in a barrel's or the saguaro's, studded with felted areoles in a prickly pear's, and with spines on those areoles in a hedgehog's, the organ pipe's or a spiny cholla's (Anderson, The Cactus Family pp. 31 to 33).

generator.params.bud_size.why: A cactus's bud is its flower closed, its pericarpel and floral tube already near their full size and its tepals swelling to open: drawn seven tenths of the open flower's width.

generator.params.bud_share.why: A cactus whose months are stated flowers in them: every place in its ring of flowers is a bud before it opens, a flower in its months and fruit after them, so none is drawn as a bud all year.

generator.params.fruit_share.why: Nor is any place drawn as fruit all year: this year's flowers become its fruit, and older fruit hang below them in older rings or chains where the species keeps them.

appearance.bodies.stem.dome.why: A cactus stem closes over as many of its tip's radii as its tip's shape says: over a length and a half where it tapers to its apex, a half sphere where it is rounded, a short shoulder under a broad top, and a low rim round a flat top nearly level with it (Flora of North America's flat-topped Astrophytum asterias and Lophophora).

appearance.bodies.stem.pit.why: A depressed top sinks to a pit at its centre, where the youngest areoles form: nearly a third of the tip's radius at its centre, below the low rim of a flat dome (Flora of North America's Lophophora, 'flat or domelike, with a deeply depressed centre'); other tops have none.

appearance.bodies.stem.shoulder.why: A tapering tip narrows steadily toward its apex, a rounded one follows a quarter circle, a broad one keeps its width into a full shoulder before turning in under its flattish top, and a flat one keeps it nearly to the rim of its level top.

generator.params.pit.why: The program sets the crown's flowers and fruit down into the pit the body draws, so it takes the same depth.

generator.params.dome.why: The program sets the crown's ring of flowers on the shoulder of the dome the body draws, so it takes the same length.

generator.params.fill.why: A column's old pieces, laid down narrow while the plant was young, fill out toward a share of the adult width: nearly all of it on a cylindrical stem, three quarters on a club-shaped one, which stays narrower at its foot than above (Gibson and Nobel, The Cactus Primer p. 79: a stem that elongates faster than it widens becomes club-shaped).

appearance.bodies.stem.tubercles.height.why: A tubercle stands from the stem as far as a flora's word for it says, as a share of the stem's radius: barely a swelling under each areole of a ribbed barrel (Anderson's Ferocactus wislizeni), low knobs along undulate ribs (F. cylindraceus), distinct knobs, or the prominent ones a cholla's joint is knobbly with.

appearance.bodies.stem.tubercles.stretch.why: A tubercle is as long along the stem, for its width, as its shape says: an ovoid one a little longer, an elongate one two to three times, a broadly oval one half as long again.

appearance.bodies.stem.tubercles.point.why: A conical tubercle comes to a point, a cylindrical one stands steep-sided, and rounded, elongate and broad ones are low mounds.

appearance.bodies.stem.spines.radial.dis.why: A joint's lower areoles carry fewer spines, or none, where its flora puts them mostly or only on the upper areoles: the share rises toward the tip, and where the lower areoles have none, the lower half of the joint is bare of spines.

appearance.bodies.stem.spines.central.di.why: The central spines keep to the upper areoles as the radials do.

appearance.bodies.stem.spines.main.dista.why: The main central keeps to the upper areoles as the other centrals do.

generator.params.flank.why: A column's flowers open in a ring round its apex, or also down its flank: near the tip and along the upper sides, on the last six years' growth, or from the upper half of a short, slow stem, on its last fifteen years'.

generator.params.ring_angle.why: A mammillaria's flowers open 'in ring distant from stem apex' (Flora of North America's Mammillaria), from the axils of tubercles grown the year before, so the ring sits most of the way down the dome rather than round the tip.

generator.params.crown_rings.why: Its fruit ripen the year after flowering, while the stem grows on, so last year's ring of fruit stands below this year's flowers: 'subsequent apical growth displacing fruits even farther away from apex' (Flora of North America's Mammillaria).

generator.params.ring_step.why: Each older ring sits a year's growth farther down the dome.

appearance.bodies.stem.tubercles.face.why: A deltoid tubercle is a flat-faced triangular plate, its tip pointing down and out, with its areole's woolly groove down the middle of its face (Flora of North America's Ariocarpus: 'tubercles arranged in rosettes or mosaics, ± triangular', 'exposed faces of tubercles strongly differentiated from sides', 'areoles elongate, forming a wide woolly groove on each tubercle'); it is wider than long ('8-20 × 11-25 mm').

appearance.bodies.stem.tubercles.fissure.why: A plate's face is nearly smooth, wrinkled, or 'deeply fissured on either side of central areolar groove, coarsely rugose' (Flora of North America's Ariocarpus fissuratus var. fissuratus).

appearance.bodies.stem.spines.radial.cri.why: Stiff needlelike radials run straight; bristles waver a little; hairlike, soft radials curl and lie every which way (Flora of North America's Mammillaria prolifera var. texana, 'hairlike, soft').

appearance.bodies.stem.axils.wool.why: Wool in a tubercle's axil makes a tuft in the crease above the tubercle about an eighth as wide as the tubercles stand apart ('axils with short wool', Flora of North America's Mammillaria heyderi), thinner where bristles share the axil.

appearance.bodies.stem.axils.bristles.why: A bristly axil bears a few slender bristles ('sparse white hairs and slender bristles', Flora of North America's Mammillaria prolifera var. texana).

appearance.bodies.stem.axils.bristle_len.why: The axil's bristles are as long as the flora says.

appearance.bodies.stem.axils.colour.why: The axils' wool and bristles take the colour the flora gives them, or else the areoles' wool's.

appearance.bodies.stem.colour.why: A cactus's skin is drawn in the colour its flora gives the stem or joints; its ribs' valleys darken it.

appearance.bodies.stem.spines.radial.col.why: The radial spines are drawn in the colour the flora gives the spines.

appearance.bodies.stem.spines.central.co.why: The central spines take the colour the flora gives them apart, else the spines' colour.

appearance.bodies.stem.spines.main.colou.why: The main central is a central spine and is coloured as they are.

appearance.bodies.stem.greying.colour.why: Old spines turn to the colour the flora gives them once grey or dark.

appearance.bodies.stem.spines.glochid.co.why: An areole's glochids are drawn in the colour its flora gives them: a beavertail's red-brown, a jumping cholla's yellow.

appearance.bodies.stem.areoles.felt.why: An areole's felt is drawn in the colour the flora gives its wool.

appearance.bodies.stem.ribs.count.why: A stem's ribs vary within the count its flora gives; the body draws more of them round a thicker stem.

appearance.bodies.stem.areoles.spacing.why: Areoles sit along a rib's crest, or over a joint, this far apart.

appearance.bodies.stem.areoles.margins.why: A flat joint whose areoles sit only along its margins, in the notches of its teeth (Britton and Rose's Zygocactus and Schlumbergera), bears none on its faces.

appearance.bodies.stem.spines.radial.cou.why: An areole bears as many radial spines as its flora counts, varying within its range.

appearance.bodies.stem.spines.radial.len.why: Floras give the longest spines; a set's spines vary a quarter either way about its length, so the longest stand about a quarter above it.

appearance.bodies.stem.spines.central.co.why: An areole bears as many central spines as its flora counts. Where one central stands apart as the main one, the others are set by hand, so the two sets together make the count.

appearance.bodies.stem.spines.central.le.why: As for the radials: the longest central stands about a quarter above the set's length.

appearance.bodies.stem.flecks.share.why: Tufts of white hairs speckle the skin between the areoles as thickly as the flora says: a sparse sprinkle (Flora of North America's Astrophytum asterias, 'sparsely speckled'), numerous specks (its Astrophytum, 'speckled by numerous tufts'), or a cover that hides the skin.

appearance.bodies.stem.spines.central.cu.why: A curved central bends back about 40° over its length, as the floras' 'curved' and 'curving' spines of a barrel or a hedgehog do; a twisted one wanders about 25° as it turns (see twist). A hook is the principal central's (a fishhook's), so the other centrals stay unhooked where the form is hooked.

appearance.bodies.stem.spines.main.curve.why: The main central bends as the floras' central spine form says, as the other centrals do.

appearance.bodies.stem.spines.central.tw.why: A twisted central turns about its length like a wrung ribbon, which shows on a flattened spine: drawn as half a turn from base to tip (Flora of North America's Echinocactus polycephalus, centrals 'often twisted').

appearance.bodies.stem.spines.main.twist.why: The main central twists as the other centrals do.

appearance.bodies.stem.spines.main.hook.why: A hooked principal central turns back at its tip as a fishhook does, 120° to 180° (Anderson's Ferocactus wislizeni and Cochemiea), drawn at the middle of that span.

appearance.bodies.stem.spines.main.lengt.why: The main central is the longest a flora gives, about a quarter above its set's length.

generator.params.radius_height.why: A barrel is globular while young (Abrams 1951's Ferocactus acanthodes, 'globular when young, becoming cylindric'; Flora of North America's Ferocactus, Astrophytum and Mammillaria, stems spheric or depressed-spheric before they lengthen): its tip widens to nearly its full width by the time it stands as tall as it is wide, so over about a third of that width of height.

generator.params.sink.why: A cactus whose contractile roots draw it down sits as deep as its flora says: not at all, a third of its stem, most of it ('mostly low and deep-seated in substrate', Flora of North America's Astrophytum), or so deep only its top shows, level with the ground ('flush with soil surface', its Astrophytum asterias).

generator.params.stems.why: A cactus clump stands on as many stems from its base as its flora counts: the geometric middle of a count as skewed as Flora of North America's '3-60-branched' (a usual clump of about a dozen, not thirty), or a few or many where it only words them; one stem where it is single.

generator.params.stem_lean.why: The stems of a clump fan out from its base, the outermost leaning from upright at about the angle its floras' words give the stems ('stems erect', 'ascending', 'spreading'), the inner ones less: a vase of columns.

generator.params.bend.why: A clump's stems hold the angle they leave the base at and turn up only a little as they grow, so an organ pipe's columns spread into a vase rather than standing as a bundle; only fastigiate stems close up toward upright.

appearance.bodies.stem.ribs.spacing.why: A grown stem bears its flora's usual count of ribs round its stated thickness (the middle of the count where no usual one is given), so they stand that far apart; a thinner, younger stem fits fewer, down to the count's least.

appearance.organs.*.shape.petal_ratio.why: A cactus's inner tepals are as broad for their length as its flora measures them ('inner tepals 37-75 x (8-)14-25 mm', Flora of North America's Echinocereus engelmannii), drawn among as many tepals as the flower bears.

traits.flowering_position.note: Wikipedia, Cactus (read 2026-10-16): flowers arise from areoles (upper part), mostly near the growing stem tips; DELTA Cactaceae: terminal or lateral. Areoles are lateral short shoots, so lateral, clustered near the apex.

traits.stamens.note: Simpson, Plant Systematics (2019) p. 374: stamens numerous, spiral or in clusters on the hypanthium (Floral Diagrams p. 192: arising centrifugally on a ring). Book writes ∞ (numerous); 200 is our stand-in for the upper bound and 20 for 'numerous' with no stated lower bound.

traits.carpels.note: Ronse De Craene, Floral Diagrams (2010) p. 192: carpels (3) 4 to 5, up to 18; Simpson p. 374 says 3 to many.

traits.spines.note: Britton and Rose's The Cactaceae (vol. 1, 1919, p. 8): every cactus has areoles, special organs in the axils of its leaves or where they would be, which bear its spines (and glochids, hairs or glands), its branches and its flowers.

traits.note: Abrams's Illustrated Flora of the Pacific States, volume 3 (1951), read in full (Cactaceae by I. L. Wiggins): perianth segments numerous, grading from sepals to petals, imbricated, their bases coalescent in a cup or tube borne on the apex of the ovary; stamens numerous, on the throat of the tube; ovary inferior, 1-celled; style 1, stigma lobes 1 to numerous. Jepson eFlora (as quoted in search results; the page itself was not read): flowers radial, rarely bilateral. No flora counts the tepals.

generator.program.note: The cacti's own program (growth plan G2.3a): columns, barrels and chains of joints, their ribs, areoles and spines from each species' look.

rules.note: Spec rework E6c: the cacti's ribs, areoles and spines grown from the characters their floras state, in each body look that has ribs or a spine set of that role. The joints of chollas, prickly pears and the jointed epiphytes from their stated form and size, for any cactus whose stem is a chain of joints.

traits.perianth_parts.note: Anderson, The Cactus Family (2001) pp. 19 and 33: the perianth is many segments grading from scale bracts through sepal-like to petal-like tepals; Kubitzki vol. 5 (2003) p. 13: spiral, partly acyclic, the parts indeterminate in number; Gibson and Nobel, The Cactus Primer p. 246: many free perianth parts arranged helically. No source counts them for the family: 15 to 60, typically 30, by hand from those words, where species and genera say no more.

traits.life_span.note: Watson and Dallwitz, The Families of Flowering Plants (DELTA data, items edited May 2026), family Cactaceae: the herbs' life form (character 21), coded perennial. Read from the coded states by script (spec-rework/b1/delta/mapdelta.py with character 21 added); states the authors do not qualify, side by side, read as often.

traits.phyllotaxis_pattern.note: Simpson, Plant Systematics (2019) p. 374, 375, 376, family Cactaceae: phyllotaxis pattern spiral; read as "spiral".

traits.leaf_division.note: Simpson, Plant Systematics (2019) p. 374, 375, 376, family Cactaceae: leaf division simple; read as "simple".

traits.inflorescence.note: Simpson, Plant Systematics (2019) p. 374, 375, 376, family Cactaceae: inflorescence solitary flowers in the axils (rarely terminal cymes), usually; read as {"solitary": "usually"}.

traits.sexual_system.note: Simpson, Plant Systematics (2019) p. 374, 375, 376, family Cactaceae: sexual system hermaphrodite (rarely unisexual), usually; read as {"hermaphrodite": "usually"}.

traits.fruit_type.note: Simpson, Plant Systematics (2019) p. 374, 375, 376, family Cactaceae: fruit type berry (rarely dry and indehiscent), usually; read as {"berry": "usually"}.

rules.generator.params.radius_height.note: How PlantGen widens a barrel (thread Cactus flowering seasons, round 5, 2026-10-19): at 1 - exp(-h / radius_height) of its width at height h, so 95% of it once as tall as wide; the floras' words (globular when young) give the shape, the third is the model's choice.

rules.generator.params.sink.note: How PlantGen sinks a stem (round 5, 2026-10-19): the column program's sink is how deep the foot of a full-grown stem lies; shares of 0.3, 0.6 and 0.85 of the stem's height for the floras' partly, mostly and flush are the model's choice, the last leaving the top sixth and the dome above ground.

rules.generator.params.stems.note: How PlantGen counts a clump's stems (round 5, 2026-10-19): the geometric mean of a stated count's least and most, as floras' counts of branches run long-tailed; 3 for few, 12 for many and 30 for a thicket where no count is given are the model's choice.

rules.generator.params.stem_lean.note: How PlantGen fans a clump (round 5, 2026-10-19): the outermost stem's lean at its foot for each word of limb_angle, about the middle of the angle the seed plants' rule gives a limb, the inner stems leaning less (column program).

rules.generator.params.bend.note: How PlantGen holds a clump's stems (round 5, 2026-10-19): a turn up of 0.06 radians a metre leaves a 3 m stem within about ten degrees of the angle it set off at; the model's choice.

rules.appearance.bodies.stem.ribs.spacin.note: How PlantGen fits ribs (round 5, 2026-10-19): the body fits round(2 pi r / spacing) ribs within the stated count, so a spacing of pi times the stated diameter over the stated (usual or middle) count gives that count on a grown stem.

rules.appearance.organs.*.shape.petal_ra.note: How PlantGen draws a tepal's breadth (round 5, 2026-10-19): the stated width over the stated length of the inner tepals, as the seed plants' rule does from a petal's outline word.
